expect.statement: After accounting for other factors, amphetamine use (amphetamine or methamphetamine) is associated with more violence in two longitudinal studies by overlapping research groups, one in the general population and one in people dependent on methamphetamine; a meta-analysis of mostly cross-sectional studies found an adjusted association in the same direction that was not statistically clear, and none of these sources can show that use came before the violence, so whether use causes violence is not settled. In a systematic review and meta-analysis, the pooled adjusted odds ratio was 1.4 (95% CI 0.8–2.4; 6 studies), against 2.2 (1.2–4.1; 10 studies, I² 95%) unadjusted. In unadjusted post hoc subgroups, violent behaviour (hostility rating scales, violent behaviour or sexual exploitation reported in surveys, and violent or self-destructive behaviour in an emergency department) was associated (3.7, 3.1–4.5) and violent offending was not clearly associated (1.0, 0.4–2.7; I² 94%). For amphetamine use disorder the review has a single study: among offenders whose punishment was reduced or waived because of mental disorder, those with the disorder had more violent re-offending over 7 years (unadjusted OR 6.2, 3.1–12.3; 52 people with the disorder; quality score 43%). The violence studies had among the lowest quality ratings in the review, with poor measurement of use; the review's authors judge that large effects in two population surveys and two longitudinal studies suggest that an association may exist but needs confirmation. The review also describes a within-person analysis of the same Australian treatment cohort as the psychosis study in section 9, in which severe hostility was more frequent during periods of use after adjustment for concurrent other drug use; that paper has not yet been read. A later general-population birth cohort, not in the review (Christchurch, New Zealand; about 1,000 people interviewed at 21, 25, 30 and 35; 28% used methamphetamine or amphetamine at least once between 18 and 35), found that use in a period went with more self-reported violence in the same period after adjustment for childhood and adolescent factors and for concurrent depression, anxiety, alcohol and cannabis use disorders, life stress, unemployment and psychotic symptoms: perpetration OR 1.60 (1.01–2.54), victimisation 1.57 (1.00–2.47), intimate-partner violence perpetration 1.55 (1.04–2.30) and victimisation 1.09 (0.80–1.49). Odds were higher among the 51 people who had used at least weekly (perpetration 4.84, 2.48–9.46), in an analysis adjusted for childhood and adolescent factors only that related the heaviest use in any period to violence at any time from 18 to 35, so the two need not fall in the same period; less frequent use was not clearly associated with perpetration (1.13 and 1.40, intervals including 1). Use and violence were reported for the same periods, so which came first is unknown, and other illicit drug use was not adjusted for. A second longitudinal study, also later than the review, followed 469 people dependent on methamphetamine in Sydney and Brisbane (mostly people entering treatment, most of whom injected; the same cohort as the hostility analysis inside the review), with reports for the past month at entry, 3 months, 1 year and 3 years (2006–2010). Self-reported crime involving violence, such as violence in a robbery or assault, was reported in 113 of 927 months with methamphetamine use (12%) and 19 of 593 months without (3%). Comparing each person's months with and without use, which removes the influence of stable personal characteristics, the odds were 8.2 times higher (4.2–15.9) unadjusted and 3.4 times higher (1.5–8.0) after adjustment for age, income, unemployment, unstable housing and concurrent alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, heroin and ecstasy use; unadjusted percentages rose with days of use, and the adjusted dose estimates are only in a supplement that has not been read. Use and crime were reported for the same month in the same interview, treatment and imprisonment during follow-up were not taken into account, and the analysis was exploratory; the authors say that their intervals are wide because few participants committed crime in months without use, and that the results apply to people dependent on methamphetamine, not to recreational use. The two longitudinal studies share three authors (McKetin, Boden, Foulds), and the second shares four with the review (McKetin, Foulds, Degenhardt, Farrell), so their agreement is not independent replication.
expect.grade.reasoning: Observational: mostly cross-sectional studies in the review, plus two longitudinal cohorts; starts low. Risk of bias −1: the review's violence studies had among the lowest quality scores (56–58%), with poor measurement of use, and both cohorts are at high risk of bias on ROBINS-E (use and violence self-reported for the same periods; no adjustment for other illicit drugs in the birth cohort; no account of treatment or imprisonment in the dependent cohort). Imprecision −1: the pooled adjusted interval includes no association (0.8–2.4), the birth cohort's fully adjusted lower limits are 1.00–1.04, and the dependent cohort's interval (1.5–8.0) rests on few months with violent crime without use. Not upgraded for dose-response or large effect (see the domain notes). Certainty very low. Relation: is associated with, rather than insufficient evidence, because the adjusted association now appears in two longitudinal cohorts, in a general population and in people dependent on methamphetamine, with intervals that exclude no association, and the review's adjusted pooled estimate points the same way; the very low rating says how uncertain this association is, and whether use causes violence is a separate question that none of the sources can settle, because use and violence were reported for the same periods. Status: replicated by the same team. The adjusted estimates agree in direction, but the two cohorts share three authors (McKetin, Boden, Foulds), the dependent-cohort paper shares four with the review (McKetin, Foulds, Degenhardt, Farrell), and the dependent cohort is the same sample as the within-person hostility analysis inside the review's pooled estimate (McKetin et al., 2014, not yet read), so the agreement is not independent replication. In the review's unadjusted data, violent behaviour and violent offending point different ways (3.7 against 1.0, with I² 94% left unexplained within offending); the dependent cohort's within-person result for self-reported violent crime runs against the unadjusted offending estimate but does not explain that heterogeneity. The rating rests on the adjusted estimates, so this is noted rather than rated down. On the reading list: McKetin et al. (2014); a systematic review of drug-administration studies of aggression (O'Malley et al., 2022, DOI list item 110).
expect.plain: Is amphetamine use, including meth, linked to violence once other factors are taken into account? Two long-term studies found a link even after other factors were taken into account, but neither can show that meth causes violence, and the two studies share authors. A review of mostly weak studies found that the link seen in raw numbers shrank and became uncertain after adjustment; in the raw numbers it was seen for violent behaviour but not clearly for violent offences. A study in New Zealand followed about 1,000 people from age 18 to 35. In periods when they used meth or speed, people were somewhat more likely to report attacking someone or being attacked, even after many other factors were taken into account. The few who had used at least weekly had higher odds, in an analysis that took fewer factors into account. A study in Australia followed 469 people dependent on meth for up to three years and compared each person's months of use with their own months without. Violent crime was reported in 12 of 100 months with meth use and 3 of 100 months without, and the link remained after age, money problems and other drug use were taken into account. But in both studies people reported use and violence for the same periods, so the studies cannot show which came first, and the Australian study did not take treatment or time in prison into account. One study that compared people with themselves found more hostility in periods of use; it has not been read yet. The review's authors think a link may exist but needs to be confirmed.

expect.statement: In one UK study of 50 pairs of full siblings, in each of which one sibling met DSM-IV-TR criteria for stimulant dependence and the other had no personal history of substance dependence other than nicotine (the supplement's enrolment criterion; the main report says no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse), both siblings had lower white-matter fractional anisotropy than 50 unrelated controls without a personal or family history of dependence, similar in age and verbal IQ, and shared three grey-matter clusters of difference from them: a larger left amygdala, a larger left putamen, and smaller volume across the left postcentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus and posterior insula. The white-matter, putamen and posterior insula differences were more alike within families than in random pairings (one-tailed permutation tests, not corrected for multiple testing); the amygdala difference was not. The imaging analyses included 146 people for grey matter and 145 for white matter; the grey-matter maps were thresholded to allow about one false-positive cluster per map, and the shared clusters are the overlap of two comparisons with the same control group. More of the non-dependent siblings than of the controls smoked (55% against 12%), and the sexes were unbalanced (51% and 64% men); a re-analysis of non-smokers kept the grey-matter differences, but no smoking check is reported for white matter, and neither this nor the single-sex re-analysis gives statistics. Differences shared by the two siblings suggest a familial vulnerability, genetic or from the shared family environment, that may predate drug use; the study cannot show that it does, because nobody was assessed before use began. Neither the main report nor its supplement names an orbitofrontal or anterior insular difference or compares the two siblings directly; a review describes a larger hippocampus in both siblings and smaller orbitofrontal and anterior insular volumes in the dependent siblings only: the hippocampal statement may come from the supplement, which labels the shared medial temporal cluster amygdala/hippocampus in places, but the orbitofrontal and anterior insular statement cannot be traced to the study. The supplement maps regions where lower fractional anisotropy and grey matter went with more years of stimulant use in the dependent siblings, without statistics or region names and without adjustment for age, which rises with years of use, or for their other dependence (55% on opiates, 26% on alcohol), so they do not separate an effect of stimulant use from these. The dependent siblings were still using stimulants when tested (urine positive in all but three); 94% were dependent on cocaine and 6% on amphetamines, and methamphetamine is not mentioned.
expect.magnitude: No cluster statistics in the main report. Supplement, Table S2 (means over voxels selected because they differed between groups, so the differences are inflated): fractional anisotropy 0.55 in controls, 0.53 in non-dependent siblings and 0.52 in dependent siblings (SD 0.02); grey matter in the shared clusters, controls against non-dependent and dependent siblings: left amygdala 0.76 against 0.81 and 0.83, left putamen 0.34 against 0.38 and 0.38, left postcentral gyrus 0.89 against 0.75 and 0.74 (editors' calculation: standardized differences of about 0.7 to 1.3). Fractional anisotropy group difference F(2,141) = 26.3, P < 0.001 (main report; 145 participants with white-matter data, so the degrees of freedom fit one covariate, sex; editors' calculation: η² about 0.27, inflated by the voxel selection). Within-family similarity (one-tailed permutation tests, uncorrected for multiple testing): white matter P = 0.004, putamen P = 0.013, posterior insula P = 0.012, amygdala P = 0.144 (not familial).
expect.plain: Brothers and sisters of people dependent on stimulants, who had never been dependent on drugs or alcohol themselves (apart from nicotine), shared some of the same brain differences from unrelated volunteers. That suggests some differences run in families and may come before drug use, although nobody was scanned before they started using. More of the brothers and sisters than of the volunteers smoked, and the check that smoking did not explain the differences covered only part of the scans. The study shows pictures of brain areas where differences were larger the longer people had used, but gives no numbers and did not separate years of use from age or from other drugs. A review reports other differences found only in the dependent person, but neither the study's report nor its supplement names them. Almost all the dependent people (94 in 100) were dependent on cocaine; the rest were dependent on amphetamines, and the study does not mention meth.
expect.grade.reasoning: One cross-sectional study of 50 sibling pairs, read in full with its supplement. Starts low (observational). Risk of bias, one level: ROBINS-E overall high on the study card: smoking was far more common in the non-dependent siblings than in the controls (55% against 12%) and was checked only for grey matter, by a re-analysis of non-smokers without statistics; the sexes were unbalanced, handled by a covariate in the behavioural analyses and by single-sex grey-matter analyses without statistics; and only the clusters shared by both sibling groups are described, with imaging values from voxels selected because they differed. Indirectness, one level: 94% of the dependent siblings were dependent on cocaine and 6% on amphetamines, and methamphetamine is not mentioned. Imprecision, one level: 50 people per group (146 and 145 in the imaging analyses); grey-matter maps thresholded to allow about one false-positive cluster per map, the shared clusters coming from two comparisons with the same control group; familiality tests one-tailed and not corrected for multiple testing (three of the six would not pass a Bonferroni threshold, editors' calculation). Certainty very low. The claim is rated as an association; whether the shared differences predate use cannot be settled by this design, and the correlations with years of use are shown only as maps, without statistics or adjustment for age.
